prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV" (ticker BUD), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "BUD", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: Anheuser-Busch InBev SA/NV
markets: Beyond Beer (ready-to-drink cocktails, hard seltzers, flavored malt beverages)
B2B digital ordering and marketplace for retailers (BEES)

mission.statement: We dream big to create a future with more cheers.
mission.source: AB InBev purpose statement, repeated in its 2026 Interim Financial Report (six months ended 30 June 2026) and on its website
mission.plain: It wants to bring people together over its drinks and keep growing that habit for the long term.

about.plain: AB InBev is the world's biggest beer company. It brews and sells famous beers like Budweiser, Corona, Michelob Ultra, Stella Artois and Modelo in many countries. It also makes canned cocktails and alcohol-free beers. Shops, bars and restaurants buy its drinks, often through its own phone app called BEES, and sell them to adults.
about.customers: Supermarkets, convenience stores, bars, restaurants and wholesalers buy its beer, and adults drink it.
about.everyday: If you have seen a Corona at the beach or a Budweiser advert during the Super Bowl, you have seen AB InBev's products.

money.part: Middle Americas beer (Mexico, Colombia, Peru and others)

money.plain: Michelob Ultra, Bud Light, Busch Light, Budweiser, Cutwater cocktails

money.part: Europe, Middle East and Africa beer

money.plain: Budweiser, Harbin, Cass in China and Korea

money.part: BEES Marketplace (third-party products sold through its ordering app)
money.plain: other companies' goods sold to small shops via BEES; GMV $1.2B in 2Q26, up 50%

result.summary: Yes. AB InBev owns 8 of the world's 10 most valuable beer brands (Kantar BrandZ 2026) and is the largest brewer by far, with unmatched scale in brewing, buying and distribution that supports a 35.8% normalized EBITDA margin (FY2025). Its weaknesses are a shrinking beer category in some markets, heavy debt and exposure to consumer backlash, as the 2023 Bud Light boycott showed.

pricingPower.evidence: FY2025 revenue per hectolitre rose 4.4% while volumes fell 2.3%, so revenue still grew 2.0% organically and normalized EBITDA margin expanded 101bps to 35.8%; in HY26 revenue/hl rose 4.3% with volumes up 0.8%. But volumes fall when prices rise and the 2023 Bud Light boycott showed brand loyalty can break quickly.

moats.evidence: Kantar BrandZ 2026 ranks Corona (#1), Budweiser (#2), Modelo (#4), Michelob Ultra (#5), Brahma, Bud Light, Skol and Stella Artois among the 10 most valuable beer brands, 8 of 10 owned by AB InBev; Michelob Ultra became the top-selling US beer by volume in 2025 (Circana).
Drinkers can switch beer brands at no cost; some stickiness comes from retailers and bars using its BEES ordering app (2Q26 GMV $15.0B) and from distributor relationships.
BEES Marketplace adds third-party products to the app retailers already use (GMV $1.2B in 2Q26, up 50%), a modest two-sided effect; the core beer business has no network effect.

As the largest brewer it buys barley, aluminium and packaging, runs breweries and buys advertising at a scale no rival matches, helping deliver $21.2B of normalized EBITDA on $59.3B revenue in FY2025.
In many markets (Mexico, Brazil, Colombia, Peru, South Africa) it holds dominant positions where national brewing and distribution networks would be uneconomic to duplicate.
It is the incumbent; craft brewers, spirits-based ready-to-drink makers and non-alcoholic upstarts are the ones counter-positioning against it.
Its zero-based budgeting cost culture, global brand-building playbook (Corona grew 17% outside Mexico in 2Q26) and route-to-market systems are refined over decades, though not impossible to copy.
It owns century-old brands and exclusive distribution networks in several countries, but no truly exclusive input or talent pool.

customers.evidence: Its brands top value and sales rankings (8 of the 10 most valuable beer brands, Kantar BrandZ 2026; Michelob Ultra the #1 US beer by volume in 2025) and it was the #1 share gainer in US total alcohol in HY26 (Circana), though the 2023 Bud Light boycott showed loyalty is fragile; no NPS data is published.

talent.evidence: Its Global Management Trainee programme and ownership-and-meritocracy culture are well known, and the CEO and most top leaders are long-tenured insiders, but no top-tier employer ranking was verified and the demanding cost culture is known for long hours.

product.evidence: Corona is the world's most valuable beer brand for the third year running (Kantar BrandZ 2026), Michelob Ultra is America's best-selling beer by volume, and its brands collect brewing awards, though beer quality is largely a matter of taste.

threats: Long-term decline in beer drinking among younger adults and moderation trends, including GLP-1 weight-loss drugs reducing alcohol consumption
Consumer boycotts and culture-war backlash, as the 2023 Bud Light controversy showed (Modelo Especial took the US #1 spot in 2023)
Share loss to spirits-based ready-to-drink cocktails, cannabis beverages and non-alcoholic alternatives
High leverage: net debt of $64.2B (2.86x normalized EBITDA) at 30 June 2026 limits flexibility if earnings fall
Emerging-market currency swings (Brazil, Mexico, Argentina, South Africa) and hyperinflation that cut reported US-dollar results
Input-cost and tariff pressure on aluminium cans and barley
Weak beer demand in China hurting Budweiser APAC
Regulation: excise tax increases, advertising limits and health warnings on alcohol

ceo.name: Michel Doukeris
ceo.background: Chemical engineering degree (Federal University of Santa Catarina), master's in marketing (Fundação Getulio Vargas), Kellogg and Wharton executive programmes; joined Ambev in 1996 and ran China/APAC and North America before becoming CEO

c1.evidence: It leads the beer industry, which is mature: FY2025 volumes fell 2.3% and revenue grew 2.0% organically.

c2.evidence: People choose its beers for brand image and availability (Corona, Michelob Ultra, Budweiser), backed by unmatched distribution, which is hard to copy, but taste preferences and fashions can shift, as Bud Light's 2023 slump showed.

c3.evidence: Budweiser, Corona and Stella Artois are household names worldwide, and AB InBev owns 8 of the 10 most valuable beer brands (Kantar BrandZ 2026), making it the default leader in beer.

c4.evidence: Its purpose "We dream big to create a future with more cheers" appears in its reports, but management is known chiefly for cost discipline and financial targets rather than a world-changing mission.

c6.evidence: “Budweiser, Bud Light, big beer”: the impression is mixed; its brands are popular and familiar, but the company is also linked with mass-market lager, the 2023 Bud Light boycott and aggressive cost cutting.

c7.evidence: Global beer is a very large but slow-growing market with flat-to-declining volumes; its growth comes from price and premium mix rather than a secular trend.

c8.evidence: It is expanding into Beyond Beer (revenue up 44% in 2Q26, led by Cutwater), non-alcoholic beer and the BEES Marketplace for third-party goods (GMV $1.2B in 2Q26), but these are small next to beer.

m1.evidence: Doukeris has set a clear strategy of category expansion, digital transformation (BEES) and premium megabrands, but it is an evolution of the beer business rather than a new vision of the future.

m2.evidence: A 30-year company insider who joined Ambev in 1996, he acts like a long-term owner within its ownership culture, but he is a hired successor, not a founder.

m4.evidence: No clear evidence either way of a servant-leadership style; the company's culture is better known for meritocracy and cost discipline.

m5.evidence: Under him the company built BEES and grew Beyond Beer and Michelob Ultra Zero, but the culture is mainly famous for efficiency rather than invention.

m6.evidence: He trained as a chemical engineer but built his career in sales and marketing, serving as global Chief Sales Officer.

m7.evidence: No controversies are attached to him personally, and the company promotes sustainability goals such as net zero by 2040, but there is no strong evidence of a mission beyond profit.

m7b.evidence: No commencement speech at a top university was found.

m8b.evidence: He keeps a relatively low public profile, without a memorable public persona.

m9.evidence: Since 2021 he has cut net debt to 2.86x EBITDA, lifted normalized EBITDA margin to 35.8% in FY2025, grown underlying EPS to $3.73 in FY2025 and $2.18 in HY26 (+22.1%) and announced a $6B share buyback in October 2025.

m10.evidence: AB InBev is famous for zero-based budgeting and the frugal 3G Capital-style culture inherited from Ambev.

c10.evidence: Beer is an enjoyable product for adults, but it does not solve major problems or greatly improve lives.

p2.evidence: Brewing beer at scale is operationally demanding but not technologically hard or important to the world.

f1.evidence: Revenue rose from $46,881M in 2020 to $59,768M in 2024 but slipped to $59,320M in 2025, as currency losses offset 2.0% organic growth.

f2.evidence: Operating margin rose from 20.5% in 2020 to 26.0% in 2025, but gross margin fell from 58.1% to 55.9%.

f3.evidence: Net debt was $64.2B at 30 June 2026 against cash of $7.7B, about 2.86x normalized EBITDA, although equity is positive at $101.2B.

f4.evidence: Profit from operations rose from $9,620M (2020) to $15,405M (2025) and operating cash flow from $10,891M to $14,883M, though both dipped in single years.

v1.evidence: Corona and Michelob Ultra lead their categories, but there is no objective reason a drinker must choose them over Heineken or Modelo-like alternatives; beer choice is largely taste and image.

v2.evidence: It is not ranked among the very best places to work; no top-tier employer ranking for AB InBev was verified.

c5.evidence: Beer drinkers, bar owners and the farmers and small shops it supplies (through BEES) would miss its brands, but other brewers would quickly fill the gap.
